original_extraction.evidence_text:
The same holds true for ‘negative’ feelings such as anger, fear, sadness, insecurity and guilt. There
are multitudes of psychological strategies to ‘get rid of such feelings. But you’ve undoubtedly
discovered that even if they go away, after a while they’re back. And then they go away again. And
then they come back again. And so on and so on. The likelihood is, if you’re like most other
humans on the planet, you’ve already spent a lot of time and effort trying to have ‘good’ feelings
instead of ‘bad’ ones—and you’ve probably found that as long as you’re not too distressed, you
can, to some degree, pull it off. But you’ve probably also discovered that as your level of distress
increases, your ability to control your feelings progressively lessens. Sadly, Myth 4 is so widely
believed that we tend to feel inadequate when our attempts to control our thoughts and feelings fail.

---

These four powerful myths provide the basic blueprint for the happiness trap. They set us up for a
struggle we can never win: the struggle against our own human nature. It is this struggle that builds
the trap. In the next chapter we will look at this struggle in detail, but first let’s consider why these
myths are so entrenched in our culture.

---

The human mind has given us an enormous advantage as a species. It enables us to make plans,
invent things, coordinate actions, analyse problems, share knowledge, learn from our experiences
and imagine new futures. The clothes on your body, the shoes on your feet, the watch on your wrist,
the chair beneath you, the roof over your head, the book in your hands—none of these things would
exist but for the ingenuity of the human mind. The mind enables us to shape the world around us
and conform it to our wishes, to provide ourselves with warmth, shelter, food, water, protection,
sanitation and medicine. Not surprisingly, this amazing ability to control our environment gives us
high expectations of control in other arenas as well.
generation_rules: Present myths about emotional control as widely held but misleading beliefs
Highlight the natural recurrence of emotions despite attempts to control them
pause_rules: Pause after describing the cycle of emotions to allow reflection on the inevitability of emotional fluctuations
original_extraction.psychological_function: To increase awareness of the cyclical nature of emotions and the limitations of emotional control, thereby reducing feelings of inadequacy.
repetition_rules: Emphasize the recurring cycle of emotions coming and going to illustrate the futility of control attempts
original_extraction.therapeutic_function: To reduce the struggle against natural human emotions by challenging myths about controlling feelings and thoughts.
voice_rules: Use explanatory and validating tone to normalize emotional experiences and struggles
